Experimental. A PowerShell script on a Windows host, for what no module covers yet. Guards say when it has already done its job.

**Experimental.** Windows support is new, and this module may change between releases.

Use `windows_powershell` for what no Windows module covers yet. Values go in `args`, and the script reads them as `$A.name`: they arrive as data, so a quote or a `$(...)` in one is just text.

## Example usage

Create a directory once:

```hcl
step "app_dir" {
  windows_powershell {
    script  = "param($A) [void][IO.Directory]::CreateDirectory($A.dir)"
    args    = { dir = "C:\\app" }
    creates = "C:\\app"
  }
}
```

Run only while a check says the work isn't done:

```hcl
step "long_paths" {
  windows_powershell {
    script = "Set-ItemProperty -LiteralPath 'HKLM:\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\FileSystem' -Name LongPathsEnabled -Value 1"
    unless = "(Get-ItemProperty -LiteralPath 'HKLM:\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\FileSystem').LongPathsEnabled -eq 1"
  }
}
```

## Arguments

| Name | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `args` | map of string | No | Values the script reads as $A.name. They reach it as data, never as code. |
| `args_wo` | map of string | No | Like args, but kept out of state: state records only args_hmac, and the values are blanked from output and errors. Use it for secrets. |
| `creates` | string | No | Skip the script while this path exists. |
| `removes` | string | No | Skip the script while this path is missing. |
| `script` | string | Yes | PowerShell script. Start it with param($A), and read arguments as $A.name rather than interpolating them into the text. |
| `timeout` | string | No | How long the script may run before it is stopped. Defaults to "30m". |
| `triggers` | dynamic | No | Any value; the script runs again whenever it changes. |
| `unless` | string | No | Skip the script while this PowerShell check holds: it holds unless it throws, its last output is $false, or a native program it ran last exited non-zero. It runs at every plan, so it must change nothing. It gets args but never args_wo, which a plan doesn't have. |

## Read-only attributes

Conn3x sets these; reference them as `conn3x_windows_powershell.<circuit>__<step>["<host>"].<name>`.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `args_hmac` | string | HMAC-SHA256 of args_wo, keyed by CONN3X_HMAC_KEY or ~/.config/conn3x/hmac.key. Null without args_wo. |
| `revision` | string | Changes each time Conn3x changes this on the host. Handlers watch it. |
| `satisfied` | bool | Whether the guards hold on the host. |
| `stderr` | string | Error output of the last run, truncated to 4 KiB. |
| `stdout` | string | Output of the last run, truncated to 4 KiB. |

A step lowers to the `conn3x_windows_powershell` resource, one instance per host, and connects with its circuit's `ssh` block.

## How it works

**Failing.** A script fails by throwing. Errors stop it by default, because `$ErrorActionPreference` is `Stop`. It also fails when the last native program it ran exits non-zero; for a tool with other success codes, such as `robocopy`, finish with `$global:LASTEXITCODE = 0`. Calling `exit` is reported as a failure: use `return` to finish early, and `throw` to fail.

**Guards.** Like `command`, the script runs when the step is created, when anything that defines it changes, and when a refresh finds its guards no longer hold. `unless` runs at every plan, with the same rights as the script, so it must change nothing. A circuit someone else wrote can act on your hosts at `plan` this way: read its `unless` checks as you would its scripts.

**Secrets.** `args_wo` stays out of the plan and state. State records only `args_hmac`, and the values are blanked from output and errors. A refresh doesn't have them, so an `unless` check that needs them sees them only during an apply. `args_hmac` is a plain keyed HMAC, not stretched the way a `password_hmac` is, so keep the HMAC key away from the state when a value is short enough to guess.

**Secrets and logging.** Where a policy turns on PowerShell's module logging, Windows records what's passed to any cmdlet. Conn3x keeps `args_wo` away from cmdlets on its way to your script, so don't pass a secret to one yourself: use a .NET method, as in `[IO.File]::WriteAllText($A.path, $A.secret)`.

**Timeouts.** A script is stopped after `timeout`. Conn3x stops the whole process tree when it cancels a run, but if the connection itself drops, as when the machine running Conn3x crashes, the script carries on running on the host.

**Connecting.** The `ssh` block works as it does on Linux, with its host key pinned or in `known_hosts`. Windows Server 2025 ships OpenSSH. Server 2022 doesn't, so bootstrapping adds it first, as the Azure example's script does. Either way, Conn3x installs its own host key as part of bootstrapping the host. `become` only checks that the login is elevated, since Windows has no sudo. `agent` and `become_password_file` are errors. Keep `user` as the bare name, such as `azadmin`, which still works after the host is promoted to a domain controller.

## Removal

Deleting a `windows_powershell` step does nothing on the host.
